title: Allah heard her
hookLine: Allah heard the woman who argued with the Prophet ﷺ about her husband, and a ruling came (58:1)

lines: A LOW, URGENT VOICE IN MEDINA.
cards: In a small room in Medina, a woman is speaking with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, low and urgent. Her husband, in anger, has said an old Arabian phrase to her: you are to me like my mother's back.
By custom, that left a wife in limbo: not divorced, so she couldn't remarry, and not a wife, so he wouldn't come near her. She has children, and she's getting older. She argues her case.
In a corner of the same house, the Prophet's wife 'A'isha can't even make out the words.

teach.b: The reports name her Khawla bint Tha'laba, and her husband Aws ibn as-Samit. She pleaded, and she complained to God. And the surah that came down opens with her.

teach.h: QAD SAMI'A ALLAH: GOD HAS HEARD.
teach.b: Pickthall: "Allah hath heard the saying of her that disputeth with thee (Muhammad) concerning her husband, and complaineth unto Allah." Qad sami'a Allah: God has heard.
The surah is named for her: Al-Mujadila, she who disputes, she who pleads her case. A whole surah, named for a woman who argued. The next verses settle the matter.
Saying that phrase doesn't make a wife into a mother; it's a wrong and false thing to say.
A man who says it and wants to return must make amends first: free a slave, or if he can't, fast two months in a row, or if he can't, feed sixty poor people.
The custom that trapped women was ended. And 'A'isha's reaction is the part people remember.

teach.h: HEARING THAT TAKES IN EVERY VOICE.
teach.b: The reports preserve her words: blessed is the One whose hearing takes in every voice.

The woman was speaking to the Prophet in a corner of my house, and I couldn't hear what she said, and God heard her from above the seven heavens. Notice what the verse doesn't do. It doesn't scold her for arguing.
It records her disputing and her complaint, and answers both. A voice too low for the next room was heard, and the answer became law for everyone after her.

how: Muslims tell the story of Khawla bint Tha'laba as an example of a woman whose plea was answered in the Qur'an; Islamic law treats zihar as forbidden and sets an expiation before a husband who said it may return to his wife.

o: she who disputes, who pleads her case
she who leaves her husband's home
she who prays alone through the night

games.q: the woman who pleaded — tap the pairs.

s: the verse scolds the woman for arguing with the Prophet
it records her pleading and her complaint, and answers both.
a whole surah is named for a woman who pleaded her case
Al-Mujadila means she who disputes or pleads.
'A'isha heard every word of the conversation
she was in the same house and couldn't make out what was said.

games.q: you're Khawla. your husband has left you in limbo with an old phrase. what do you do?
o: go to the Prophet, plead your case, and complain to God.
games.why: she pleaded and complained to God, and the opening of Al-Mujadila came: God has heard. the custom was ended.

practice: Think of one thing you've been quietly unhappy about but haven't said, at home, at work, with a friend, and picture Khawla, low-voiced and steady.
Shape what you need into one calm, clear sentence, no blame, just the truth of it; if you pray, bring it to God first, as she did.

wordCard.voice: Al-Mujadila: she who disputes, the surah named for Khawla, whose complaint to the Prophet, God says, he heard. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: God has heard. The first words of Surah Al-Mujadila.

carryVoice: Your line: she was heard. The week ran from the water you drink and the purified, through Al-Hadid's nearness, soft hearts, play and iron, to Khawla's quiet voice. Day six hundred sixteen.

sources.q: Allah hath heard the saying of her that disputeth with thee (Muhammad) concerning her husband, and complaineth unto Allah.
